question:
Select the most appropriate 'one word' for the expression given below.
A professional rider in horse race.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Jockey.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Jockey" is a professional rider in a horse race, especially one who rides as a profession. (घुड़दौड़ का पेशेवर सवार)

◦ Example: The jockey guided the horse skilfully to win the derby.

• Jockeys are trained professionals who are hired by horse owners to compete in official races.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Horse Pilot" — not a standard English term; there is no such recognised one-word substitution.

• Option 2: "Cellar" (तहखाना): an underground room used for storage, unrelated to horse racing.

• Option 4: "Autocrat" (निरंकुश शासक): a ruler who has absolute power, unrelated to horse racing.

NOTE

• Other one-word substitutions related to professions/sports often asked in SSC: "Equestrian" (a horse rider in general), "Referee" (one who supervises a game), "Umpire" (one who officiates in cricket/tennis).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Eagerly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Avidly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Avidly" means eagerly or enthusiastically; with great keenness. (उत्सुकता से)

◦ Example: The children avidly waited for the ice-cream van to arrive.

• The word "eagerly" and "avidly" both convey an intense, keen desire or interest in doing something.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Perfunctorily" (लापरवाही से): done routinely and with little interest or care — nearly opposite in meaning to "eagerly".

• Option 2: "Plainly" (स्पष्ट रूप से): in a clear and simple manner; unrelated to eagerness.

• Option 4: "Neatly" (साफ-सुथरे ढंग से): in a tidy, orderly manner; unrelated to eagerness.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Eagerly" useful for SSC: "Keenly", "Zealously", "Enthusiastically", "Fervently".

• Do not confuse "Avidly" with "Avoidably" — the two look similar but have entirely different meanings.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
In a recent study,
P. little free time like a single parent nurse caring for
Q. more than one child and working long hours are
R. we showed that people on low incomes with
S. set to lose out most as energy prices rise
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. RPQS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence begins with the fixed opener "In a recent study,", so the arrangement must logically complete this opening.

• Sequencing the parts: R ("we showed that people on low incomes with") logically follows the opener since it introduces the subject "we showed that...". P ("little free time like a single parent nurse caring for") follows R, giving an example of a low-income person. Q ("more than one child and working long hours are") continues describing the nurse's situation and supplies the plural verb "are". S ("set to lose out most as energy prices rise") completes the sentence with the main predicate.

• Reading the complete sentence: "In a recent study, we showed that people on low incomes with little free time like a single parent nurse caring for more than one child and working long hours are set to lose out most as energy prices rise." This is grammatically complete and logically coherent.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: SPQR is incorrect because it places "set to lose out most..." immediately after the opener, before the subject of the sentence has even been introduced, breaking the logical flow.

• Option 3: PQSR is incorrect because it starts with an example ("little free time...") before the main clause "we showed that people..." has been stated.

• Option 4: RQSP is incorrect because it disconnects "more than one child and working long hours are" (Q) from its description of the nurse's caring role (P), which must appear together.

NOTE

• In sentence-rearrangement (para jumble) questions, always locate the part that logically follows the given opening line and identify pronoun/verb agreement clues (like the plural "are" in Q) to fix the correct sequence.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Atmospheric rivers are long, narrow bands of moisture in the atmosphere that extends from the tropics to higher latitudes.
option_1: Atmospheric rivers are long, narrow bands
option_2: of moisture in the atmosphere that extends from the
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. "of moisture in the atmosphere that extends from the".

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is the plural noun "Atmospheric rivers", and the verb inside the relative clause must agree with the noun it modifies.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement in a relative clause: the verb inside a clause introduced by "that" must agree with the noun immediately preceding "that" — here, "bands" (plural), not "moisture" or "atmosphere".

• Since "bands...that" requires a plural verb, "extends" is wrong and must be corrected to "extend". This error lies within the segment "of moisture in the atmosphere that extends from the".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Atmospheric rivers are long, narrow bands" is grammatically correct — the plural subject correctly takes the plural verb "are".

• Option 3: "tropics to higher latitudes." is grammatically correct; it merely completes the prepositional phrase "from...to...".

• Option 4: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist, as explained above, within segment 2.

NOTE

• Watch for a singular noun placed close to "that" (like "moisture" or "atmosphere" here) — it is a common SSC trap intended to distract from the true plural antecedent ("bands") that the verb must agree with.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
The mayor said to the marshals, "Don't conduct any drill tomorrow."
option_1: The mayor ordered the marshals not to conduct any drill the previous day.
option_2: The mayor ordered the marshals not to conduct any drill tomorrow.
option_3: The mayor ordered the marshals not to conducted any drill the next day.
option_4: The mayor ordered the marshals not to conduct any drill the next day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The mayor ordered the marshals not to conduct any drill the next day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The direct sentence is a negative imperative sentence ("Don't conduct...") spoken as a command/order, so the reporting verb "said to" changes to "ordered", and the structure becomes "ordered + object + not + to + V1".

• Rule — Narration of Imperative Sentences: Direct: Subject + said to + Object, "Don't + V1..." → Indirect: Subject + ordered/commanded + Object + not to + V1...

• Rule — Change of Time Expressions: since the reporting verb is in the past tense, the time expression "tomorrow" in direct speech changes to "the next day" in indirect speech.

• Applying both rules: "said to the marshals" → "ordered the marshals"; "Don't conduct" → "not to conduct"; "tomorrow" → "the next day". This gives: The mayor ordered the marshals not to conduct any drill the next day.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "the previous day" is the wrong time-expression change; "tomorrow" must become "the next day", not "the previous day".

• Option 2 is incorrect because it retains "tomorrow" unchanged, which is not allowed once the tense shifts to the past in reported speech.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "not to conducted" wrongly uses the past participle "conducted" after "to"; the infinitive must always take the base form: "not to conduct".

NOTE

• Common time-expression changes for narration: today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day/the day before; now → then; here → there; this → that; these → those; ago → before.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Monstar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Monster", not "Monstar" — a large, frightening imaginary creature, or a cruel person.

◦ Example: The film showed a terrifying sea monster.

• Spelling key: the word ends in -ster, not -star; do not confuse it with the unrelated word "star".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Letter" is correctly spelt — a written message, or a character of the alphabet.

• Option 3: "Scatter" is correctly spelt — to throw or spread things in different directions.

• Option 4: "Transparent" is correctly spelt — allowing light to pass through; easily seen through or understood.

NOTE

• Other commonly confused "-ster" endings in SSC spelling questions: gangster, minster, roadster, youngster — remember the ending is always "-ster", never "-star".

question:
Fill in the blank with the most suitable word.
One may ______ what he only holds in trust; he shares what is his own.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. allocate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Allocate" means to assign or distribute something for a particular purpose, especially when acting as a trustee or administrator over something that is not one's own. (आवंटित करना)

◦ Example: The trustee may allocate the funds held in trust for the beneficiaries' education.

• The sentence contrasts two situations: what one merely holds in trust (i.e., manages on another's behalf) one may only allocate (assign/distribute in an administrative sense), whereas what is genuinely one's own one can freely share.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Appellate" (अपीलीय): relating to appeals in a court of law; it is an adjective and does not fit grammatically or contextually as a verb here.

• Option 2: "Apply" (लागू करना): to put into operation or make use of; it does not capture the sense of distributing something held in trust.

• Option 3: "Appropriate" (विनियोजित करना): here used loosely as a verb meaning to set aside for a purpose, but it more strongly implies taking something for one's own use, which clashes with the idea of merely holding something "in trust".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "allocate" (to assign/distribute) with "allot" (to give as a share) and "appropriate" (to take for oneself, often improperly) — all three are frequently tested together in SSC vocabulary sets.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
Containing more words than necessary
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Verbose.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Verbose" means containing more words than necessary; wordy. (शब्दाडंबरपूर्ण)

◦ Example: The professor's verbose explanation confused more students than it helped.

• The word comes from the Latin verbosus, from verbum meaning "word".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Revenant" (पुनरागत): a person who returns, especially supposedly from the dead; unrelated to wordiness.

• Option 3: "Laconic" (संक्षिप्त): using very few words; this is actually the opposite of the given meaning.

• Option 4: "Platonic" (आध्यात्मिक/निष्काम): describing a relationship that is affectionate but not sexual; unrelated to wordiness.

NOTE

• "Laconic" and "Verbose" are antonyms frequently tested together in SSC — laconic = using few words, verbose = using too many words. Other related one-word substitutions: "Terse" (brief and to the point), "Garrulous" (excessively talkative).

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
She forgot the papers in the car.
option_1: The papers was forgotten by her in the car.
option_2: The papers had been forgotten by her in the car.
option_3: The papers are forgotten by her in the car.
option_4: The papers were forgotten by her in the car.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The papers were forgotten by her in the car.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "She forgot the papers in the car" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the papers" becomes the subject; being plural it takes "were"; the verb "forgot" becomes the past participle "forgotten"; and "she" becomes the object of the preposition, changing to "her".
◦ Passive: The papers were forgotten by her in the car.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was forgotten" wrongly uses the singular auxiliary "was" with the plural subject "the papers"; it should be "were".

• Option 2 is incorrect because "had been forgotten" is the passive form of the Past Perfect Tense, not the Simple Past Tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "are forgotten" is the passive form of the Simple Present Tense, which changes the meaning/tense of the original sentence.

NOTE

• Always match the auxiliary verb (was/were) to the number of the new subject (singular/plural) when converting active sentences to passive voice.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
One who does not know reading or writing
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Illiterate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Illiterate" means one who does not know how to read or write. (निरक्षर)

◦ Example: Adult literacy programmes aim to help illiterate people learn to read.

• The prefix "il-" (a variant of "in-") means "not", added to "literate" (able to read and write) to form its opposite.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Scholar" (विद्वान): a person with advanced knowledge in a particular subject; opposite in sense to the given phrase.

• Option 3: "Erudite" (विद्वतापूर्ण): having or showing great knowledge acquired from reading; opposite in sense.

• Option 4: "Fastidious" (दुराग्रही/नुक्ताचीनी करने वाला): very attentive to detail and hard to please; unrelated to literacy.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions with the "il-/in-" negative prefix: "Illegible" (not able to be read, of handwriting), "Illegal" (not lawful), "Innumerable" (too many to count).

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
To be in two minds
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. In a dilemma.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To be in two minds" means to be undecided or unable to choose between two options; to be in a state of indecision. (दुविधा में होना)

◦ Example: She was in two minds about accepting the new job offer.

• The idiom draws on the image of a person's mind being pulled in two different directions at once, unable to settle on one.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To migrate" (प्रवास करना): to move from one place to settle in another; unrelated to indecision.

• Option 2: "To be less effective" (कम प्रभावी होना): to have reduced impact or result; unrelated to indecision.

• Option 4: "To be over confident" (अति आत्मविश्वासी होना): to have excessive confidence in oneself; this is nearly the opposite of being undecided.

NOTE

• Other idioms of indecision commonly tested in SSC: "To sit on the fence" (to avoid taking sides), "To blow hot and cold" (to keep changing one's opinion), "At a crossroads" (at a point where an important decision must be made).

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Objurgation
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Endorsement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Objurgation" means a harsh rebuke or severe scolding; strong criticism. (कड़ी फटकार)

• Its antonym "Endorsement" means a public statement of approval or support for something. (समर्थन)

◦ Example: The new policy received the full endorsement of the committee, in contrast to the objurgation it had faced earlier from critics.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Hamper" (बाधा डालना): to hinder or obstruct the progress of something; unrelated in meaning, neither synonym nor antonym.

• Option 3: "Reproof" (भर्त्सना): an expression of blame or disapproval — this is actually a synonym of "objurgation", not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Commination" (धमकी/शाप): the act of threatening divine vengeance or denouncing; again a synonym of "objurgation", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Words of "rebuke/criticism" family often tested together: reproof, reprimand, censure, commination, objurgation — all synonyms — versus their antonyms praise, endorsement, commendation, approval.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
The snowstorm will __effect thousand__ of travellers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. affect thousands.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment contains two separate errors that must both be corrected.

• Rule 1 — "Affect" vs "Effect": "Affect" is a verb meaning to influence, while "Effect" is normally a noun meaning a result. Since the sentence needs a verb after "will" ("will _____ thousands of travellers"), the verb "affect" is required, not the noun "effect".

• Rule 2 — Countable noun after "thousand of": the phrase "thousand of travellers" is grammatically incomplete; when "thousand" is followed by "of + plural noun" to indicate an indefinite large number, it must itself be pluralised: "thousands of travellers".

• Applying both corrections together gives: "The snowstorm will affect thousands of travellers."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "effect thousands" is incorrect because it still uses the noun "effect" instead of the required verb "affect".

• Option 3: "affected thousand" is incorrect because the main verb "will" must be followed by the base form "affect", not the past form "affected"; also "thousand" remains wrongly singular.

• Option 4: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original sentence does contain errors, as explained above.

NOTE

• Common confusable pairs tested in SSC "sentence improvement": affect/effect, accept/except, adapt/adopt, principal/principle, stationary/stationery.

• "Hundred/thousand/million" stay singular only when preceded by a specific number (e.g. "two thousand travellers"); they take the plural "-s" and are followed by "of" when the quantity is indefinite (e.g. "thousands of travellers").

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A remedy for all ills
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Panacea.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Panacea" means a solution or remedy for all difficulties or diseases; a cure-all. (सर्वरोगहर औषधि)

◦ Example: Increasing the police force alone is not a panacea for the crime problem.

• The word comes from the Greek panakeia, from pan- ("all") + akos ("remedy").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Libertine" (स्वच्छंद व्यक्ति): a person who behaves without moral restraint, especially in sexual matters; unrelated to remedies.

• Option 3: "Convalescent" (स्वास्थ्यलाभ करने वाला): a person who is recovering from illness; not a remedy itself.

• Option 4: "Rustic" (देहाती): relating to the countryside; simple and unsophisticated; unrelated to remedies.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: "Elixir" (a magical or medicinal potion), "Antidote" (a remedy to counteract a poison), "Nostrum" (a quack remedy).

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
It turns out that my father isn't alone.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "It turns out that my father isn't alone." is examined part by part: "It turns out" is a correct present-tense idiomatic expression meaning "it is revealed/discovered"; "that my father" correctly introduces the noun clause with the possessive adjective "my" before the noun "father"; and "isn't alone" is a grammatically correct contracted negative form of "is not alone".

• Rule: the expression "It turns out that..." is always followed by a full clause (subject + verb), and no article/preposition is required before "alone", since "alone" functions correctly here as a predicate adjective.

• Since subject-verb agreement ("father isn't"), tense, and word order are all correct, the sentence has no grammatical error.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "that my father" is grammatically correct as explained above; it is not the source of any error.

• Option 3: "It turns out" is a correct, standard idiomatic opening and is not erroneous.

• Option 4: "isn't alone." is grammatically correct — "is" agrees with the singular subject "father" and "alone" is used correctly as a predicate adjective.

NOTE

• "No error" questions test whether a sentence is already correct — always check each segment individually for subject-verb agreement, tense, and preposition usage before concluding there is no error; do not assume an error must exist just because the sentence is broken into parts.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Adequate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Wanting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Adequate" means sufficient or satisfactory for a particular purpose; enough. (पर्याप्त)

• Its antonym "Wanting", when used as an adjective, means lacking in something necessary; deficient or insufficient. (कमी वाला/अपर्याप्त)

◦ Example: Despite his efforts, his preparation was found wanting just before the exam.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Indolent" (आलसी): habitually lazy; unrelated to sufficiency.

• Option 2: "Superficial" (सतही): existing or occurring at or on the surface, not thorough; unrelated to sufficiency.

• Option 4: "Taunting" (ताना मारने वाला): mocking or jeering at someone; unrelated to sufficiency.

NOTE

• Other antonyms of "Adequate" useful for SSC: "Insufficient", "Deficient", "Inadequate", "Scanty".

• Note that "Wanting" here is used as a predicate adjective (as in "found wanting"), not as the verb "wanting" (desiring).

question:
Select the word that is opposite in meaning (ANTONYM) to the word given below.
Celestial
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Terrestrial.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Celestial" means relating to the sky or heavens; heavenly. (आकाशीय/स्वर्गीय)

• Its antonym "Terrestrial" means relating to the earth or land, as opposed to the sky or sea. (पार्थिव/भूमि संबंधी)

◦ Example: Astronomers distinguish celestial bodies like stars and planets from terrestrial features found on Earth.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Heavenly" (स्वर्गीय): relating to heaven or the sky; this is actually a synonym of "celestial", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Divine" (दिव्य): of or like God or a god; again close in meaning to "celestial", not an antonym.

• Option 4: "Stellar" (तारकीय): relating to a star or stars; also close in meaning to "celestial", not an antonym.

NOTE

• Word family: celestial, heavenly, divine, stellar are near-synonyms relating to the sky/heavens, while terrestrial, earthly, mundane relate to the earth — a frequently tested antonym pair in SSC.

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: I do not require any technical knowlege or expertice.
option_2: I do not require any technical knowledge or expertise.
option_3: I do not requir any technical knowledge or expertice.
option_4: I do not require any technichal knowledge or expertise.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. I do not require any technical knowledge or expertise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correctly spelt sentence contains "knowledge" and "expertise" correctly spelt, and "require" correctly spelt.

• Spelling key: "knowledge" = know + ledge (remember the silent "d" before "ge"); "expertise" ends in -tise, not -tice.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "knowlege" and "expertice" are both misspelt; the correct spellings are "knowledge" and "expertise".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "requir" and "expertice" are both misspelt; the correct spellings are "require" and "expertise".

• Option 4 is incorrect because "technichal" is misspelt; the correct spelling is "technical" (no "h" after the "c").

NOTE

• Commonly misspelt words in SSC "choose the correct spelling" questions: knowledge, expertise, technical, require, occurrence, questionnaire, embarrass.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. some 81 percent of the reefs in the area had become severely bleached
Q. warm seawater were particularly brutal in the northern part of
R. Australia's famous Great Barrier Reef, where surveys reported that
S. from late 2015 to the middle of 2016, the effects of overly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. SQRP.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence has no fixed opener given, so the parts must be arranged to form one continuous, logical sentence on their own.

• Sequencing the parts: S ("from late 2015 to the middle of 2016, the effects of overly") sets up the time frame and subject; Q ("warm seawater were particularly brutal in the northern part of") continues the subject "overly warm seawater" with its verb "were...brutal"; R ("Australia's famous Great Barrier Reef, where surveys reported that") names the location and introduces a further reported clause; P ("some 81 percent of the reefs in the area had become severely bleached") completes the reported clause with the specific finding.

• Reading the complete sentence: "From late 2015 to the middle of 2016, the effects of overly warm seawater were particularly brutal in the northern part of Australia's famous Great Barrier Reef, where surveys reported that some 81 percent of the reefs in the area had become severely bleached." This is grammatically complete and logically coherent.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: SPQR is incorrect because it inserts P ("some 81 percent...had become severely bleached") too early, before the location and the "surveys reported that" clause that must introduce it.

• Option 3: QRPS is incorrect because it begins with "warm seawater were particularly brutal", omitting the necessary time-frame opener (S), leaving "overly" without its noun phrase.

• Option 4: PSQR is incorrect because it opens with the reported finding (P) before either the time frame or the subject of the sentence has been established.

NOTE

• When no fixed opening line is given, look for the part containing the earliest logical anchor (such as a time expression, as in S here) to identify the true starting sentence part.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
To meet one's water loo
option_4: To be badly defeated in a contest
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To be badly defeated in a contest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To meet one's Waterloo" means to be decisively defeated, especially after a period of success; to suffer a final, crushing defeat. (करारी हार का सामना करना)

◦ Example: The champion finally met his Waterloo in the final round of the tournament.

• The idiom originates from the Battle of Waterloo (1815), where Napoleon Bonaparte suffered his final, decisive defeat, ending his rule.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To meet one's look alike" (अपने जैसे दिखने वाले से मिलना): to encounter someone who resembles oneself; unrelated to defeat.

• Option 2: "To realize one's mistake" (अपनी गलती का एहसास होना): to become aware of an error one has made; unrelated to defeat.

• Option 3: "To face the reality" (वास्तविकता का सामना करना): to accept facts as they are; unrelated to decisive defeat specifically.

NOTE

• Other idioms derived from historical events/battles common in SSC: "To cross the Rubicon" (to take an irrevocable step), "To fiddle while Rome burns" (to be occupied with trivial matters during a crisis).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.
The difference between the solar radiation absorbed and the thermal radiation emitted to space (1) ________ radiation budget of the earth. Since there is no appreciable long-term trend in planetary temperature, it may be (2) ________ that this budget is essentially zero on a global long term average.
The rate of temperature change in any region is directly (3) ________ to energy budget of the region and inversely proportional to its heat capacity. While the radiation (4) ________ may dominate the average energy budget of many surfaces, nonradiative energy transfer and storage also are (5) ________ important when local changes are considered.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. determines.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb that shows the difference between absorbed solar radiation and emitted thermal radiation fixes or defines the radiation budget of the earth.
